prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and of its active form, which made incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity possible

statement.case_for: My final position is a single-part B045 prize to Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. I opened with Knudsen and moved to Mojsov in round 1; nothing in the exchange has moved me back. The reasoning is the same as before. The prize rests on a discovery chain: incretin physiology and human GLP-1 action (Holst), proglucagon processing and receptor biology (Drucker), and identification of the active truncated GLP-1(7-36) peptide (Mojsov). The therapies are the proof of significance. The mechanism is confirmed by independent outcome trials for glycaemia, weight, and cardiovascular and renal disease, so maturity is not in doubt. Five other members arrived at the same trio on their own reasoning, which I do not count as an argument. What persuades me is that when each of us explains why Mojsov should hold the third seat, the answer is the same scientific one: the active form had to be identified before the pharmacology could be built.
statement.case_against: The attribution risk has not gone away. Mojsov's priority over the active form is contested against Habener, who is outside the credited names, and none of us can settle this from the supplied record, so I will not pretend the trio is clean. Excluding Knudsen also has a real cost. The prize could be read as stopping short of the therapy, and the citation can only acknowledge her work indirectly through the phrase on therapies. I also keep the concern that the commercial scale of semaglutide and tirzepatide inflates how original the underlying science looks. Against that, every alternative I considered carries its own credit problem (B003 with Zhou and parallel VLP groups, B006 with six names, B025 with Eshhar uncredited). None gives a better-defined prize this year.

responses.point: Sten holds Mojsov over Knudsen, wants the citation to refer to therapies built on the discoveries, and says the committee should check the primary literature on the active peptide before the final ballot. If her claim proved weaker than assumed he would revisit the trio.
responses.response: I agree with the principle and I now share his trio. I would put the condition more narrowly than he does. The check he asks for is not something we can run in this round, since we only have the supplied materials. So the committee should decide now what it will do if the doubt remains. My answer is that the doubt alone does not remove Mojsov. A contested priority over one step still leaves a distinct, real contribution, and Habener's claim, even if valid, would bear on who shares that step and does not erase the step. I would reopen the trio only on affirmative evidence that the active-peptide identification was made by someone else and not by her.

responses.point: Thomas would put Knudsen in only if the citation is meant to cover the drugs themselves, and wants that choice stated openly.
responses.response: That is a fair test, and on it I choose the discovery citation. The wording I propose names the physiology and the active form and says they made the therapies possible. This is a deliberate choice and I am stating it: we are crediting identification over drug design. I still would not call Knudsen's acylation merely industrial, since extending a two-minute half-life to days needed a real mechanistic idea, but that is development on an established mechanism and our precedent leans toward the discovery that opened the field. I accept his point that this is a judgement about what the prize is for, and that the science alone does not settle it.

responses.point: Rickard ranks optogenetics fifth because it is mainly a research tool, while saying the six-name attribution problem is the main reason it sits below cleaner candidates. She also raises a two-part prize with B015 and a reduced GLP-1.
responses.response: I have read her round-1 reply and I now agree that the attribution is the real obstacle for B006. Six names and a cap of three exclude Bamberg, Boyden and Miesenböck, and Rickard and Wahren-Herlenius disagree about which trio best reflects the discovery. I still disagree that the lack of a clinical endpoint counts against it. A two-part B045 plus B015 would cut B045 to one or two names and would force the exact exclusion I most want to avoid. I would sooner keep GLP-1 whole at three and treat the UPR as an independent case for a later year, since its Walter and Mori pair is the cleanest on the list.

responses.point: Per says the Knudsen swap would leave the active peptide uncredited and tilt the prize toward a company programme, and notes that five of six of us landed on Mojsov. He also ranks B006 below B003 and B015 for attribution reasons.
responses.response: I accept the first point, and it is why I moved. The swap rewards the clearest causal path to the drugs but leaves out a scientific step the pharmacology depended on. I treat the five-of-six count as weak evidence, since our reasoning could be correlated, but it is consistent with the argument and does not conflict with it. On B006 I concede his attribution argument, and I have kept B003 and B015 as my two alternatives and dropped B006. I am not changing my view that optogenetics is a discovery in the physiological sense; I just do not think it can be credited cleanly under the three-person cap.

responses.point: Marie says that if Mojsov's claim is judged unresolvable, a pair of Holst and Drucker is a better fallback than swapping in a developer, and that the committee should discuss this openly. She also supports B003 as lead if B045 stalls on credit.
responses.response: I think her fallback is the more honest one and I would adopt it over my own round-1 swap. If the committee concludes that Mojsov cannot be credited, then Holst and Drucker alone, with the same citation, is better than adding Knudsen, because it avoids rewarding the industrial route in place of a contested discovery. I would not go that way now, because the evidence for Mojsov's contribution to the active form is strong enough that omitting her would also be an error. On B003, I agree that the Lowy and Schiller L1 VLP work is the secure core and that Zhou and the parallel groups are a real attribution risk. If B045 fails, B003 is where I would go first.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's priority for the active peptide form relative to Habener holds up. I cannot resolve this from the supplied record and have not seen primary documents.
Whether the committee wants the prize for the physiology and peptide discovery only, or also for drug design, and whether the citation wording can acknowledge Knudsen without crediting her.
Whether the HPV attribution (Frazer, Zhou, parallel VLP groups) can be resolved well enough to make B003 a real fallback.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. I disclose a 2009 co-authored paper with Thomas Perlmann and work with Sten Grillner and Patrik Ernfors, but none of them is credited on a shortlisted ballot, so I see no basis for recusal. I work in motor-circuit neuroscience, where optogenetics is widely used, but I am not a candidate and have no documented tie to B006 or any other shortlisted name. I have no connection to Drucker, Holst, Mojsov, Knudsen or Habener.
